Paragraph: Having crossed the formidable Himalayas and watched his brothers and Draupadi fall one by one along the arduous journey, Yudhishthira stood at the gates of Heaven accompanied only by a stray dog that had followed him faithfully from Hastinapura. Indra descended in his celestial chariot and invited the righteous king to ascend to Heaven in his mortal body, but on one condition: he must abandon the stray dog. Yudhishthira steadfastly refused, saying: 'O King of Gods, this dog has been my loyal companion when all others fell away. To abandon one who is devoted, frightened, or seeking refuge for the sake of my own personal happiness and heavenly luxury would be a heinous sin. I do not desire a Heaven that requires me to betray a faithful creature.' Surrendering his own salvation rather than sacrificing his ethical integrity, Yudhishthira proved that his compassion extended to all living beings without condition.
Chapter/Canto/Verse_Reference: Mahaprasthanika Parva, Section 3 (often cataloged alongside Svargarohana Parva)
Situation/Problem_Faced: At the threshold of ultimate spiritual attainment and eternal peace, Yudhishthira faces an acute ethical dilemma between personal salvation (entering Heaven) and uncompromising moral integrity (refusing to abandon a vulnerable, loyal animal).
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Yudhishthira chooses radical empathy, loyalty, and moral consistency over ego-driven reward, rejecting celestial paradise if it requires compromising his core ethical principles.
Outcome/Resolution: The dog reveals itself to be Dharma Deva (the deity of righteousness), testing Yudhishthira one last time; Yudhishthira passes the ultimate test of moral integrity and enters Heaven in his mortal form.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dharmic Empathy (Universal compassion extending beyond human-centric morality to all sentient beings)
Sharanagata-Raksha (The sacred duty to protect and remain loyal to those who seek refuge)
Nishkama Virtue (Practicing righteousness without expectation of reward or fear of loss)
Atma-Samyama (Supreme self-mastery overriding personal ambition in favor of ethical truth)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Yudhishthira's final test embodies the pinnacle of 'Dharma'—demonstrating that true righteousness is not about reaching a destination (Heaven) but maintaining absolute compassion, integrity, and non-betrayal ('Sharanagata-Raksha') even when offered the highest personal reward.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This passage highlights high moral maturity, value-congruent decision-making, and profound psychological resilience. Yudhishthira demonstrates an internalized locus of control and authentic self-esteem, refusing to sacrifice his core values for social validation or systemic rewards, illustrating how deep empathy protects an individual from moral injury.
